keyFacts: A permutation counts arrangements where order matters: nPr = n! / (n - r)!
A combination counts selections where order does not matter: nCr = n! / (r! x (n - r)!).
nPr is always greater than or equal to nCr for the same n and r.
nCr = nC(n - r): choosing r is the same as leaving out n - r.
Both n and r must be whole numbers with 0 <= r <= n.
Permutations and combinations are the foundation of probability calculations.

permutation-and-combination-calculator.quickAnswer: Permutations count arrangements where order matters; combinations count groups where it does not. nPr equals n! divided by (n-r)!, and nCr equals n! divided by r! times (n-r)!. Pick the one that matches whether order matters in your question.
permutation-and-combination-calculator.workedExample:
A committee of 3 people is chosen from 10 candidates.

Order does not matter, so use combinations:
nCr = 10! / (3! x 7!) = (10 x 9 x 8) / (3 x 2 x 1) = 720 / 6 = 120.

There are 120 possible committees.

If instead the 3 people win gold, silver and bronze (order matters):
nPr = 10! / 7! = 10 x 9 x 8 = 720 possible medal arrangements.
